messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: rstan: plot comments and questions
parts:
2 technical issues and a substantive puzzle.

Technical #1: plot(stanfit) has little dots on each bar. Are they the
median for each chain? It would be good to document.

Technical #2: Also, the coloring underneath each parameter includes
colors that are not in the key. I see (when things go badly) some dark
red. The key has a brown or dark tan as the value for both >=2 and NaN.

Substantive: Finally, the traceplots look weird to me. One of the
chains (in orange if the attachment comes through) gets semi-stuck with
small variation. The region it is getting stuck in has better log
probability than shown in most of the other chains. It also has
unusually low beta (the intercept) and high variability in the prior for
the beta. The probability should be relatively insensitive to changes
in beta in the range it gets "stuck" in since the poisson parameter is
exp(beta) and that is close to zero.

In an earlier run with a somewhat misspecified model there was more
dramatic stickiness, in which one of the chains had a likelihood that
bounced around relatively a lot, flattened out for a significant period,
and then started bouncing again.

So I guess generically this is a sign that something might be wrong in
the model. If it's real, would it indicate the probability distribution
is multi-modal?

I'd really appreciate comments from those with more experience about
what this means.

This is an intercept only poisson model with inflation at 1 and
variability associated with individuals and clusters. Using development
code from a bit before the 2.0 release.

My original specification had completely separate terms for individual
and cluster variation. It performed extremely badly; the traceplots
showed 2 problems: first, one of the chains was just stuck (though at a
much higher lp__ than the others); second the 2 forms of variation were
clearly playing off each other. So I switched to a parameterization in
terms of total variation (individual + cluster) and a parameter giving
the split of total variation into the 2 components.

This also incorporates what I hope is a correct specification of a
likelihood with censoring (from a different thread).

data {
int<lower=0> N; // number of respondents
int<lower=0> NCLUSTER; //number of clusters
int iCluster[N]; // cluster id
vector[N] x; // covariates--just an intercept in this case
int<lower=1,upper=10> mnDetail[N]; // outcome
}
parameters {
real<lower=0,upper=1> theta; // fraction monogamous. implicit uniform prior.
real beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients
real<lower=0> sigma_beta; // hyperprior for beta
vector[NCLUSTER] alpha_raw; // cluster effects
vector[N] gamma_raw; // individual effects
real<lower=0> sigma_total; //individual+cluster variance
real<lower=0,upper=1> gamma_share;
}
transformed parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma; // cluster effects
real<lower=0> sigma_gamma; //individual effects
real beta;
vector[NCLUSTER] alpha;
vector[N] gamma;
sigma <- sqrt(1.0-gamma_share)*sigma_total;
sigma_gamma <- sqrt(gamma_share)*sigma_total;
beta <- beta_raw*sigma_beta;
alpha <- alpha_raw*sigma;
gamma <- gamma_raw*sigma_gamma;
}
model {
vector[N] beta_x;
sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5);
sigma_total ~ cauchy(0, 5);
beta_raw ~ uniform(-5, 5);
alpha_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
gamma_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
// mnDetail is in [1, 10]
// We allow some probability of monogamy and then treat mnDetail-1 as poisson, with top-coding
for (n in 1:N) {
beta_x[n] <- (x[n] * beta)+alpha[iCluster[n]]+gamma[n];
if (mnDetail[n] == 1)
increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(bernoulli_log(1, theta), bernoulli_log(0, theta) + poisson_log_log(0, beta_x[n])));
else {
increment_log_prob(bernoulli_log(0, theta));
if (mnDetail[n] < 10)
increment_log_prob(poisson_log_log(mnDetail[n]-1, beta_x[n]));
else
increment_log_prob(poisson_ccdf_log(8, exp(beta_x[n])));
}
}
}

On 10/23/13 5:33 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> 2 technical issues and a substantive puzzle.
>
> Technical #1: plot(stanfit) has little dots on each bar. Are they the
> median for each chain? It would be good to document.

Yes, and I believe it is documented somewhere. Do you mean there should
be a caption on the plot itself?

> Technical #2: Also, the coloring underneath each parameter includes
> colors that are not in the key. I see (when things go badly) some dark
> red. The key has a brown or dark tan as the value for both >=2 and NaN.

I think an easier to parse color scheme would help. I can't tell what's
what in the current color scheme.

> Substantive: Finally, the traceplots look weird to me. One of the
> chains (in orange if the attachment comes through) gets semi-stuck with
> small variation. The region it is getting stuck in has better log
> probability than shown in most of the other chains. It also has
> unusually low beta (the intercept) and high variability in the prior for
> the beta. The probability should be relatively insensitive to changes
> in beta in the range it gets "stuck" in since the poisson parameter is
> exp(beta) and that is close to zero.

This is a feature, not a bug, as Michael Betancourt's been trying to
explain. And in your case, it's confounded by the fact that the mode is
often not close to the posterior mean; and when you jump closer to the
mode [which is unlikely], it's also unlikely to jump back.

> In an earlier run with a somewhat misspecified model there was more
> dramatic stickiness, in which one of the chains had a likelihood that
> bounced around relatively a lot, flattened out for a significant period,
> and then started bouncing again.
That's what should happen. It's just maintaining detailed balance.

> So I guess generically this is a sign that something might be wrong in
> the model. If it's real, would it indicate the probability distribution
> is multi-modal?

What makes you think it's multimodal rather than just varying in scale?

You see this same kind of behavior with the funnel. It takes a long time
to find the neck of the funnel, and when it does, it takes a long time
to get back out.

> I'd really appreciate comments from those with more experience about
> what this means.

You can often fix the model by tightening the priors so values stay away
from where you don't want them to be. But in some sense, it's not broken
as is.

> This is an intercept only poisson model with inflation at 1 and
> variability associated with individuals and clusters. Using development
> code from a bit before the 2.0 release.
>
> My original specification had completely separate terms for individual
> and cluster variation. It performed extremely badly; the traceplots
> showed 2 problems: first, one of the chains was just stuck (though at a
> much higher lp__ than the others); second the 2 forms of variation were
> clearly playing off each other. So I switched to a parameterization in
> terms of total variation (individual + cluster) and a parameter giving
> the split of total variation into the 2 components.
>
> This also incorporates what I hope is a correct specification of a
> likelihood with censoring (from a different thread).

It's certainly easier to follow this way --- it matches the generative
process more cleanly (first choose monogamy, then choose value).

I'm afraid you're going to need better help than mine to control the
model more.

- Bob

parts:
The issue is probably with sigma_beta, not beta itself. Scale parameters like this tend to
be heavy-tailed in complex models which causes problems with HMC and various
ergodicity expectations.

Try increasing the target acceptance probability,

sample->adapt->delta

from the nominal value of 0.65 to, say, 0.9, 0.99, and 0.999. If this indeed the problem
you should see the dispersion of sigma_beta grow and finally stabilize. For your final fit
take the smallest target acceptance probability that yields consistent results.

>>

>>> is multi-modal?
>>
>> What makes you think it's multimodal rather than just varying in scale?
>
> The fact that the "unusual" region had higher probability than most of
> the rest made me think the other chains were trapped around a local
> maximum. "Trapped" = unlikely to jump out of that region.
>
> Exactly what scale would be varying?

Read the description of the funnel. The scale of the lower level
parameters in a hierarchical model varies with the higher-level scale
parameter. E.g.,

for (n in 1:N0
beta[n] ~ normal(0,sigma);

sigma ~ ...

When sigma is low, the scale of beta is different thna when it's high.
The neck of the funnel has low sigma and the big open part a high sigma.

It's hard to jump into the neck and hard to jump out.

>>
>> You see this same kind of behavior with the funnel. It takes a long time
>> to find the neck of the funnel, and when it does, it takes a long time
>> to get back out.
>>
>>> I'd really appreciate comments from those with more experience about
>>> what this means.
>>
>> You can often fix the model by tightening the priors so values stay away
>> from where you don't want them to be. But in some sense, it's not broken
>> as is.
>
> Would that mean, tightening around the unusual region with high
> probability?

No, tightening away from that region, which may not be possible.
One of Andrew's grad students, Vince Dorie, has written on this topic
for point estimates, but some of the same issues come up for MCMC.

A Non-Degenerate Penalized Likelihood Estimator for Variance Parameters in Multilevel Models
Yeojin Chung, Sophia Rabe-Hesketh, Vincent Dorie, Andrew Gelman, and Jingchen Liu.

It's in Psychometrika, which I don't think is open, but there's a draft
here:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/draft4_12.pdf

The point here is keeping the estimates away from 0, which will
completely trap a point estimate.

> intercepts also have low n_eff). I'll try his advice once I figure

> understand what the acceptance probability is--I'm a bit puzzled
> because in Metropolis the acceptance probability is an outcome rather
> than being directly tunable (I think). Ahh... is is that the tuning
> aims for a particular acceptance rate?

You tune the acceptance probability in a standard random walk Metropolis
by adjusting the step size. Lower step size = higher acceptance probability.
See, for example, Andrew's most famous theory paper:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/baystat5.pdf

which is summarized in the recent MCMC handbook he co-edited.

Michael's working on generalizations for HMC --- there's a basic result
for multivariate normals by Roberts et al., but it doesn't apply to hierarchical
models.

You should see the variance/intervals of sigma_beta grow as you increase the target acceptance probability.

Exactly -- you're really decreasing the step size and allowing easier transitions into the tails.

settings you want to generate something like the attached figure and really see the intervals for latent parameters
like sigma_beta stabilize,

>> Hmh, it is less efficient, but it appears sigma_beta's upper tail continues to widen.
> Q3 is now 1.57.
>
> tree depth is basically pinned at 10 and n_eff min dropped to 37, that
> value being associated with sigma. .5 hour wall time. sigma_beta n_eff = 761

Never let the tree depth saturate at the maximum -- just increase the threshold and your effective
samples sizes should shoot right back up.

> OTOH, the estimates for the parameters of interest have basically been
> the same since the first runs. I'm not sure they are stable (over
> different acceptance rates), but if they're moving it's not by much

It can be tricky with hierarchical models, as the heavy tails in latent parameters also translates
into heavy tails in the derived parameters but not as extreme. It tends to manifest in rare but
significant "extreme" events -- the saturation of tree depth may be preventing you from seeing
these events, or it may be that your model is particularly well-behaved. Either way, the only way
to be sure is to see that all estimates have stabilized.
